plain_english: Don't let someone else's unnatural behavior become your problem. You weren't built to be miserable alongside others or to suffer when they suffer. You were built to be happy with them. If someone is unhappy, remember that their unhappiness is their own fault. God made all people to be happy and free from inner turmoil. He gave us the tools for this. Some things belong to each person. Other things don't. Some things can be blocked, forced, or taken away — these don't belong to you. But the things that can't be interfered with — those are yours. And whether something is good or evil? God made that yours too. He did this because he cares for us and protects us like a father.
original_excerpt: Let not that which in another is contrary to nature be an evil to you; for you are not formed by nature to be depressed with others nor to be unhappy with others, but to be happy with them. If a man is unhappy, remember that his unhappiness is his own fault; for God has made all men to be happy, to be free from perturbations. For this purpose he has given means to them, some things to each person as his own, and other things not as his own; some things subject to hindrance and compulsion and deprivation; and these things are not a man's own; but the things which are not subject to hindrances, are his own; and the nature of good and evil, as it was fit to be done by him who takes care of us and protects us like a father, he has made our own.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: But you say, "I left someone, and now they're upset." Why did they think you belonged to them? When they looked at you and felt happy, why didn't they also remember that you're mortal? That it's natural for you to leave for another country? They're suffering because of their own foolishness. But why are you crying? What's the point of feeling sorry for yourself? Have you not thought about these things either? Like useless women, you enjoyed everything that gave you pleasure as if it would last forever — places, people, conversations. And now you sit there weeping because you don't see the same faces or live in the same places.
original_excerpt: But you say, I have parted from a certain person, and he is grieved. Why did he consider as his own that which belongs to another? why, when he looked on you and was rejoiced, did he not also reckon that you are a mortal, that it is natural for you to part from him for a foreign country? Therefore he suffers the consequences of his own folly. But why do you or for what purpose bewail yourself? Is it that you also have not thought of these things? but like poor women who are good for nothing, you have enjoyed all things in which you took pleasure, as if you would always enjoy them, both places and men and conversation; and now you sit and weep because you do not see the same persons and do not live in the same places.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: You deserve to be more miserable than crows and ravens. They can fly wherever they want. They can change nests. They can cross oceans without crying or regretting what they left behind. But wait — they do this because they don't think like we do. So did the gods give us reason just to make us unhappy and miserable? Are we supposed to spend our lives being wretched and complaining? Should everyone live forever? Should no one ever travel? Should we never leave home but stay rooted like plants? And when a friend travels, should we sit around crying? Then when they come back, should we dance and clap like little children?
original_excerpt: Indeed you deserve this, to be more wretched than crows and ravens who have the power of flying where they please and changing their nests for others, and crossing the seas without lamenting or regretting their former condition. Yes, but this happens to them because they are irrational creatures. Was reason then given to us by the gods for the purpose of unhappiness and misery, that we may pass our lives in wretchedness and lamentation? Must all persons be immortal and must no man go abroad, and must we ourselves not go abroad, but remain rooted like plants; and if any of our familiar friends goes abroad, must we sit and weep; and on the contrary, when he returns, must we dance and clap our hands like children?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: But my mother grieves when she doesn't see me. Why hasn't she learned these principles? I'm not saying we shouldn't try to prevent her grief. I'm saying we shouldn't desperately want to control what isn't ours to control. Another person's sorrow belongs to them. My sorrow belongs to me. I'll stop my own sorrow by any means necessary, because that's in my power. I'll try to help with another person's sorrow as much as I reasonably can. But I won't try to control it completely. If I do that, I'll be fighting against God. I'll be opposing Zeus and setting myself against the way the universe works. The punishment for this fight against God and this disobedience won't just fall on my children's children. I'll pay for it myself, day and night. I'll be startled by dreams, disturbed, trembling at every bit of news, and my peace of mind will depend on other people's letters.
original_excerpt: But my mother laments when she does not see me. Why has she not learned these principles? and I do not say this, that we should not take care that she may not lament, but I say that we ought not to desire in every way what is not our own. And the sorrow of another is another's sorrow; but my sorrow is my own. I then will stop my own sorrow by every means, for it is in my power; and the sorrow of another I will endeavor to stop as far as I can; but I will not attempt to do it by every means; for if I do, I shall be fighting against God, I shall be opposing Zeus and shall be placing myself against him in the administration of the universe; and the reward (the punishment) of this fighting against God and of this disobedience not only will the children of my children pay, but I also shall myself, both by day and by night, startled by dreams, perturbed, trembling at every piece of news, and having my tranquillity depending on the letters of others.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Someone has come from Rome. I just hope nothing bad happened. But what harm can reach you when you're not even there? Someone comes from Greece. I hope nothing bad happened there either. This way, every place in the world becomes a source of worry for you. Isn't it enough to be miserable where you actually are? Do you have to be miserable about places across the sea too, just because of some letter? Is this what you call having your life under control? So suppose my friends died in distant places. What happened to them except what happens to all humans? How can you want to live to old age and also never see anyone you love die?
original_excerpt: Some person has arrived from Rome. I only hope there is no harm. But what harm can happen to you, where you are not? From Hellas (Greece) some one is come; I hope that there is no harm. In this way every place may be the cause of misfortune to you. Is it not enough for you to be unfortunate there where you are, and must you be so even beyond sea, and by the report of letters? Is this the way in which your affairs are in a state of security? Well then suppose that my friends have died in the places which are far from me. What else have they suffered than that which is the condition of mortals? Or how are you desirous at the same time to live to old age, and at the same time not to see the death of any person whom you love?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Don't you know that over a long life, all kinds of things will happen? Fever will kill one person. A robber will kill another. A tyrant will kill someone else. This is how the world works. This is what the people around us face. Cold and heat, unhealthy living, travel by land and sea, storms, and countless other circumstances — they destroy one person, exile another, send one on a diplomatic mission and another to war. So don't sit there panicking about all these things. Don't sit there crying, miserable, calling yourself unlucky, depending on others — and not just one or two people, but thousands and thousands of them.
original_excerpt: Know you not that in the course of a long time many and various kinds of things must happen; that a fever shall overpower one, a robber another, and a third a tyrant? Such is the condition of things around us, such are those who live with us in the world; cold and heat, and unsuitable ways of living, and journeys by land, and voyages by sea, and winds, and various circumstances which surround us, destroy one man, and banish another, and throw one upon an embassy and another into an army. Sit down then in a flutter at all these things, lamenting, unhappy, unfortunate, dependent on another, and dependent not on one or two, but on ten thousands upon ten thousands.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Didn't you hear this when you studied with the philosophers? Didn't you learn this? Don't you know that human life is like being at war? One person has to stand guard. Another has to go out and spy. A third has to fight. Not everyone can be in the same place. And it wouldn't be better if they were. But you ignore the general's orders. Then you complain when something harder than usual gets assigned to you. You don't see what you're doing to the army. If everyone copies you, no one will dig trenches. No one will build walls. No one will keep watch or put themselves in danger. Everyone will be useless as soldiers.
original_excerpt: Did you hear this when you were with the philosophers? did you learn this? do you not know that human life is a warfare? that one man must keep watch, another must go out as a spy, and a third must fight? and it is not possible that all should be in one place, nor is it better that it should be so. But you neglecting to do the commands of the general complain when anything more hard than usual is imposed on you, and you do not observe what you make the army become as far as it is in your power; that if all imitate you, no man will dig a trench, no man will put a rampart round, nor keep watch, nor expose himself to danger, but will appear to be useless for the purposes of an army.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Say you're on a ship as a sailor. You can't just stay in one spot and refuse to move. If the captain orders you to climb the mast, you can't refuse. If he tells you to run to the front of the ship, you can't refuse. What ship captain would put up with you? He'd throw you overboard as a useless burden and a bad example to the other sailors. Life works the same way. Everyone's life is like being at war — a long war with many battles. You must do your duty like a soldier. Follow every command from your general. If you can, try to figure out what he wants before he even asks. But this general we serve in life is nothing like an earthly general. He's far stronger and far superior in character.
original_excerpt: Again, in a vessel if you go as a sailor, keep to one place and stick to it. And if you are ordered to climb the mast, refuse; if to run to the head of the ship, refuse; and what master of a ship will endure you? and will he not pitch you overboard as a useless thing, an impediment only and bad example to the other sailors? And so it is here also: every man's life is a kind of warfare, and it is long and diversified. You must observe the duty of a soldier and do every thing at the nod of the general; if it is possible, divining what his wishes are; for there is no resemblance between that general and this, neither in strength nor in superiority of character.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Don't you know that a good person doesn't act for show? They act because it's right. What's the benefit of doing the right thing? What's the benefit to someone who writes the name 'Dion' correctly? The benefit is that they wrote it correctly. Isn't there a reward then? Do you want a bigger reward for being good than simply doing what's good and just? At the Olympics, you don't want anything more than winning. Being crowned at the games seems like enough. Does being good and happy seem like such a small, worthless thing to you? The gods brought you into this world for these purposes. Now it's your job to do the work of an adult. Do you still want nurses and mommy? Will you let foolish women make you weak with their crying? Will you never stop being a foolish child? Don't you know that the older someone gets, the more ridiculous they look acting like a child?
original_excerpt: Know you not that a good man does nothing for the sake of appearance, but for the sake of doing right? What advantage is it then to him to have done right? And what advantage is it to a man who writes the name of Dion to write it as he ought? The advantage is to have written it. Is there no reward then? Do you seek a reward for a good man greater than doing what is good and just? At Olympia you wish for nothing more, but it seems to you enough to be crowned at the games. Does it seem to you so small and worthless a thing to be good and happy? For these purposes being introduced by the gods into this city (the world), and it being now your duty to undertake the work of a man, do you still want nurses also and a mamma, and do foolish women by their weeping move you and make you effeminate? Will you thus never cease to be a foolish child? know you not that he who does the acts of a child, the older he is, the more ridiculous he is?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Here's how to handle this: when you kiss your child, your brother, or your friend, don't let your feelings run wild. Don't let your joy go wherever it wants. Hold it back. Control it like those people who stand behind generals during victory parades and whisper "remember, you're mortal." You do the same thing. Remind yourself that the person you love will die. What you love doesn't really belong to you. It's been given to you for now — not permanently, and not forever. It's like a fig or grapes that come in their season. If you want figs in winter, you're being foolish. So if you want your son or friend when they're gone, know that you're asking for figs in winter. Winter is to figs what death is to the people we lose — it's just the natural order.
original_excerpt: So in this matter also: if you kiss your own child, or your brother or friend, never give full license to the appearance ([Greek: phantasian]), and allow not your pleasure to go as far as it chooses; but check it, and curb it as those who stand behind men in their triumphs and remind them that they are mortal. Do you also remind yourself in like manner, that he whom you love is mortal, and that what you love is nothing of your own; it has been given to you for the present, not that it should not be taken from you, nor has it been given to you for all time, but as a fig is given to you or a bunch of grapes at the appointed season of the year. But if you wish for these things in winter, you are a fool. So if you wish for your son or friend when it is not allowed to you, you must know that you are wishing for a fig in winter. For such as winter is to a fig, such is every event which happens from the universe to the things which are taken away according to its nature.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Here's another thing: when you're enjoying something, remind yourself it won't last forever. What's wrong with kissing your child and whispering, "Tomorrow you might die"? Or saying to a friend, "Tomorrow one of us will leave and we'll never see each other again"? You say these are unlucky words. Some spells are unlucky too. But if they help us, who cares? As long as they're useful. What makes words unlucky anyway — just that they point to something bad? Cowardice is an unlucky word. So is pettiness, sadness, grief, and shamelessness. These are all unlucky words. But we shouldn't be afraid to say them if they protect us from the actual things. Are you telling me that any word describing something natural is bad luck?
original_excerpt: And further, at the times when you are delighted with a thing, place before yourself the contrary appearances. What harm is it while you are kissing your child to say with a lisping voice: To-morrow you will die; and to a friend also: To-morrow you will go away or I shall, and never shall we see one another again? But these are words of bad omen—and some incantations also are of bad omen; but because they are useful, I don't care for this; only let them be useful. But do you call things to be of bad omen except those which are significant of some evil? Cowardice is a word of bad omen, and meanness of spirit, and sorrow, and grief, and shamelessness. These words are of bad omen; and yet we ought not to hesitate to utter them in order to protect ourselves against the things. Do you tell me that a name which is significant of any natural thing is of evil omen?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Say that even harvesting corn is a bad sign, because it means destroying the ears of corn — but not destroying the world. Say that leaves falling is also a bad sign. Say that dried figs replacing fresh figs is bad, and grapes becoming raisins is bad. All these things are just changes from one state to another. They're not destruction — they're part of a fixed system and natural order. Going away from home is like this — a small change. Death is like this too — a bigger change. You don't go from existing to not existing. You go from what you are now to something you're not now. Will I stop existing then? You won't exist as you are, but you'll become something else that the world needs. You didn't choose when to come into existence either. You came when the world needed you.
original_excerpt: say that even for the ears of corn to be reaped is of bad omen, for it signifies the destruction of the ears, but not of the world. Say that the falling of the leaves also is of bad omen, and for the dried fig to take the place of the green fig, and for raisins to be made from the grapes. For all these things are changes from a former state into other states; not a destruction, but a certain fixed economy and administration. Such is going away from home and a small change: such is death, a greater change, not from the state which now is to that which is not, but to that which is not now. Shall I then no longer exist? You will not exist, but you will be something else, of which the world now has need; for you also came into existence not when you chose, but when the world had need of you.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Keep these ideas ready at all times — day and night. Write them down. Read them. Talk about them with yourself and others. Ask people: Can you help me with this? Then go ask someone else, and someone else. When something happens that you don't like, this thought will help you right away: it's not a surprise. It makes a huge difference to be able to say: I knew I had a mortal son.
original_excerpt: Let these thoughts be ready to hand by night and by day; these you should write, these you should read; about these you should talk to yourself and to others. Ask a man: Can you help me at all for this purpose? and further, go to another and to another. Then if anything that is said be contrary to your wish, this reflection first will immediately relieve you, that it is not unexpected. For it is a great thing in all cases to say: I knew that I begot a son who is mortal.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: You'll say to yourself: I knew I would die someday. I knew I might have to leave home. I knew I could be kicked out. I knew I might go to prison. When you turn around and look at yourself, ask where this thing that happened came from. You'll quickly remember it comes from things outside your control — things that aren't really yours. So what is it to me? Then you'll ask the most important question: Who sent this? The leader? The general? The state? The law? Give it to me then. I must always obey the law in everything.
original_excerpt: For so you also will say: I knew that I am mortal, I knew that I may leave my home, I knew that I may be ejected from it, I knew that I may be led to prison. Then if you turn round and look to yourself, and seek the place from which comes that which has happened, you will forthwith recollect that it comes from the place of things which are out of the power of the will, and of things which are not my own. What then is it to me? Then, you will ask, and this is the chief thing: And who is it that sent it? The leader, or the general, the state, the law of the state. Give it me then, for I must always obey the law in everything.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: When something looks bad and upsets you — and you can't stop that first reaction — fight back with reason. Beat it. Don't let it grow stronger or drag you into its consequences by painting whatever pictures it wants in your mind. If you're stuck in Gyara, don't fantasize about the good life in Rome. Don't think about all the pleasures someone had there or all the pleasures you'd have if you went back. Focus on this: how should a brave person live in Gyara? Live like that. And if you're in Rome, don't daydream about life in Athens. Think only about life in Rome.
original_excerpt: Then, when the appearance (of things) pains you, for it is not in your power to prevent this, contend against it by the aid of reason, conquer it: do not allow it to gain strength nor to lead you to the consequences by raising images such as it pleases and as it pleases. If you be in Gyara, do not imagine the mode of living at Rome, and how many pleasures there were for him who lived there and how many there would be for him who returned to Rome; but fix your mind on this matter, how a man who lives in Gyara ought to live in Gyara like a man of courage. And if you be in Rome, do not imagine what the life in Athens is, but think only of the life in Rome.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Instead of chasing other pleasures, focus on this one: knowing that you're obeying God. Not just talking about it, but actually doing what a wise and good person does. What a feeling it is to say to yourself: "Right now, while others sit in schools talking seriously about virtue and saying things that sound strange to most people, I'm actually living it. They sit around discussing my good qualities, asking about me, praising me. And Zeus wanted me to prove something to myself — to know for myself whether he has the kind of soldier he needs, the kind of citizen he needs. He's chosen me to show the rest of humanity something about the things beyond our control: Look, you're afraid for no reason. You foolishly want what you want. Don't look for good things in external stuff. Look for it in yourselves. If you don't, you won't find it."
original_excerpt: Then in the place of all other delights substitute this, that of being conscious that you are obeying God, that not in word, but in deed you are performing the acts of a wise and good man. For what a thing it is for a man to be able to say to himself: Now whatever the rest may say in solemn manner in the schools and may be judged to be saying in a way contrary to common opinion (or in a strange way), this I am doing; and they are sitting and are discoursing of my virtues and inquiring about me and praising me; and of this Zeus has willed that I shall receive from myself a demonstration, and shall myself know if he has a soldier such as he ought to have, a citizen such as he ought to have, and if he has chosen to produce me to the rest of mankind as a witness of the things which are independent of the will: See that you fear without reason, that you foolishly desire what you do desire; seek not the good in things external; seek it in yourselves: if you do not, you will not find it.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: God leads me here and there for a purpose. Sometimes he shows me to people as poor, powerless, and sick. He sends me to exile, throws me in prison. But not because he hates me — God could never hate his best servants. And not because he doesn't care about me — he doesn't neglect even the smallest things. He does this to train me and to use me as an example for others. Since I'm appointed to this job, why should I care where I am? Or who I'm with? Or what people say about me? Shouldn't I focus completely on God and his instructions and commands?
original_excerpt: For this purpose he leads me at one time hither, at another time sends me thither, shows me to men as poor, without authority, and sick; sends me to Gyara, leads me into prison, not because he hates me—far from him be such a meaning, for who hates the best of his servants? nor yet because he cares not for me, for he does not neglect any even of the smallest things; but he does this for the purpose of exercising me and making use of me as a witness to others. Being appointed to such a service, do I still care about the place in which I am, or with whom I am, or what men say about me? and do I not entirely direct my thoughts to God and to his instructions and commands?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power

plain_english: Keep these ideas always ready. Practice them by yourself. Keep them sharp. Then you'll never lack something to comfort and strengthen you. It's not shameful to go without food. But it is shameful not to have enough reason to keep away fear and sadness. Once you're free from sadness and fear, what tyrant can touch you? What can his guards do? What about Caesar's attendants? Will getting some court appointment still hurt you? Will you feel pain watching others sacrifice at the Capitol when they get promoted — you who have received such great authority from Zeus? Just don't show off about it or brag. Show it through your actions. And if no one notices, be satisfied that you yourself are healthy and happy.
original_excerpt: Having these things (or thoughts) always in hand, and exercising them by yourself, and keeping them in readiness, you will never be in want of one to comfort you and strengthen you. For it is not shameful to be without something to eat, but not to have reason sufficient for keeping away fear and sorrow. But if once you have gained exemption from sorrow and fear, will there any longer be a tyrant for you, or a tyrant's guard, or attendants on Cæsar? Or shall any appointment to offices at court cause you pain, or shall those who sacrifice in the Capitol on the occasion of being named to certain functions, cause pain to you who have received so great authority from Zeus? Only do not make a proud display of it, nor boast of it; but show it by your acts; and if no man perceives it, be satisfied that you are yourself in a healthy state and happy.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Moved by a Desire of Those Things Which Are not in Our Power
